1.note: The terms **peoples**, **nations**, and **languages** mean similar things. Nebuchadnezzar is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the many different people groups]

Here, **languages** represents the people who speak them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and language groups]

This is a conventional greeting at the start of a letter that expresses the hope that all is well with the recipients. (The term **peace** has the sense of “welfare” here.) Use the equivalent greeting from your culture. The UST models one way to do that.

3.q: אָת֨וֹ⁠הִי֙ כְּ⁠מָ֣ה רַבְרְבִ֔ין וְ⁠תִמְה֖וֹ⁠הִי כְּ⁠מָ֣ה תַקִּיפִ֑ין
3.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [How very great and mighty are his miraculous signs!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **kingdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He rules as king forever]

3.q: מַלְכוּתֵ⁠הּ֙ מַלְכ֣וּת עָלַ֔ם וְ⁠שָׁלְטָנֵ֖⁠הּ עִם־דָּ֥ר וְ⁠דָֽר
3.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, indeed, he rules over people from generation to generation]

Nebuchadnezzar is using the phrase **with generation and generation** as a common expression of the culture to mean “for all generations” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [continuing throughout all generations]

4.q: אֲנָ֣ה נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּ֗ר שְׁלֵ֤ה הֲוֵית֙ בְּ⁠בֵיתִ֔⁠י וְ⁠רַעְנַ֖ן בְּ⁠הֵיכְלִֽ⁠י
4.note: Here Nebuchadnezzar is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.
In this context, **house** may represent “royal house” or “kingdom.” The UST follows that interpretation.

5.q: חֵ֥לֶם חֲזֵ֖ית וִֽ⁠ידַחֲלִנַּ֑⁠נִי וְ⁠הַרְהֹרִין֙ עַֽל־מִשְׁכְּבִ֔⁠י וְ⁠חֶזְוֵ֥י רֵאשִׁ֖⁠י יְבַהֲלֻנַּֽ⁠נִי
5.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [I saw a dream that terrified and alarmed me as I lay on my bed]

Nebuchadnezzar is using the phrase **the visions of my head** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the things that he saw while he was dreaming.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the things I saw in my dream]

6.note: The expression **was set** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I set a decree]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the dream signified]

8.note: Here Nebuchadnezzar is introducing **Daniel** as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a man named Daniel came in before me]
The word **Belteshazzar** is the Babylonian name that Nebuchadnezzar gave to Daniel, based on the name of one of his own gods.

Nebuchadnezzar is using the possessive form to describe a **spirit** that is characterized by **the holy gods**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a divine spirit from the holy gods]

9.note: Nebuchadnezzar begins to report the words that he spoke to Daniel without using a verb such as “said” to introduce them. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **visions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [tell me what I saw in my dream]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **interpretation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and tell me what it means]

10.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **visions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I saw in my mind]

10.q: חָזֵ֣ה הֲוֵ֔ית וַ⁠אֲל֥וּ אִילָ֛ן בְּ⁠ג֥וֹא אַרְעָ֖⁠א
10.note: Nebuchadnezzar is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that he saw a tree in his vision. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I was looking, and listen, I saw a tree in the midst of the earth]

Nebuchadnezzar is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [I saw]

11.note: The terms **became great** and **it became strong** mean similar things. Nebuchadnezzar is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [became very great]

11.q: וְ⁠רוּמֵ⁠הּ֙ יִמְטֵ֣א לִ⁠שְׁמַיָּ֔⁠א וַ⁠חֲזוֹתֵ֖⁠הּ לְ⁠ס֥וֹף כָּל־אַרְעָֽ⁠א
11.note: Nebuchadnezzar says **its height reached to the heavens, and its sight, to the end of all of the earth** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and it grew extremely tall, and it could be seen from very far away]

12.note: The expression **was fed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and all flesh got food from it]

Nebuchadnezzar is using **all flesh** to represent all living creatures. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [every living creature]

13.note: Nebuchadnezzar is using **I was looking in the visions of my head upon my bed** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I was dreaming.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I was dreaming] or [Images passed through my mind as I lay sleeping]

Nebuchadnezzar is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [I saw]
This expression describes a holy being who watches (waits) for instructions from God, that is, a holy angel, as in the UST.

14.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and thus he was ordering them to cut down the tree]

The watcher is saying what he wants the beast and the birds to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [The beast must flee from beneath it, and the birds, from its branches]

The watcher is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and let the birds flee from its branches]

14.q: גֹּ֤דּוּ אִֽילָנָ⁠א֙ וְ⁠קַצִּ֣צוּ עַנְפ֔וֹ⁠הִי אַתַּ֥רוּ עָפְיֵ֖⁠הּ וּ⁠בַדַּ֣רוּ אִנְבֵּ֑⁠הּ תְּנֻ֤ד חֵֽיוְתָ⁠א֙ מִן־תַּחְתּ֔וֹ⁠הִי וְ⁠צִפְּרַיָּ֖⁠א מִן־עַנְפֽוֹ⁠הִי
14.note: The implied word “you” in these commands is plural because the watcher is addressing the other heavenly beings who carry out his commands, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

15.note: The word “you” is implied in the command **leave** and is plural here because the watcher is speaking to the other heavenly beings, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The purpose of this **band** was to prevent the heat of the sun from splitting the tree and killing it completely. If the stump remained intact, it might send out new shoots. If your readers would not be familiar with the practice of banding a tree stump, you could explain it in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

The second instance of “grass” refers to grass in general. The first instance of “grass” refers to new grass or tender grass, that is, grass that has just started growing. If your language has its own term for this, it would be appropriate to use it here in your translation, here and in verse 23.

The expression **be wet** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And let the dew of the heavens make it wet]

16.q: לִבְבֵ⁠הּ֙ מִן־אנוש⁠א יְשַׁנּ֔וֹן וּ⁠לְבַ֥ב חֵיוָ֖ה יִתְיְהִ֣ב לֵ֑⁠הּ וְ⁠שִׁבְעָ֥ה עִדָּנִ֖ין יַחְלְפ֥וּן עֲלֽוֹ⁠הִי
16.note: The watcher is saying what he wants to happen to the man represented by the tree. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that his heart be changed from a man and that the heart of a beast be given to him and that seven times pass over him] or [His heart should be changed from a man’s, and the heart of a beast should be given to him, and seven years should pass over him]

16.q: לִבְבֵ⁠הּ֙ מִן־אנוש⁠א יְשַׁנּ֔וֹן וּ⁠לְבַ֥ב חֵיוָ֖ה יִתְיְהִ֣ב לֵ֑⁠הּ
16.note: The expressions **be changed** and **be given** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let them change his heart from a man, and let them give the heart of a beast to him]

The pronoun **his** refers to the man whom the tree represents. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Let the heart of the man whom the tree represents be changed from a man]

Here the watcher is speaking as if the man’s mind were his **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Let his mind be changed from a man]

The implication is that **seven times** refers to a fixed period of time, either seven years or seven seasons. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and let seven fixed periods of time pass over him]

17.q: בִּ⁠גְזֵרַ֤ת עִירִין֙ פִּתְגָמָ֔⁠א וּ⁠מֵאמַ֥ר קַדִּישִׁ֖ין שְׁאֵֽלְתָ֑⁠א
17.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [The watchers and holy ones have decided this together]

The speaker for **the watchers** is using the adjective **the living** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are alive]

The watcher is using the adjective **the lowest** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and he sets up over it a man who is of the lowest status]

18.note: The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [since the spirit of the holy gods is in you]

Nebuchadnezzar is using **all before that ** as a common expression of the culture to mean “since.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [since all of the wise men of my kingdom]

19.note: Daniel is using the expression **for the ones hating you and its interpretation, for your enemies** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I wish that what the dream predicts would happen to your enemies rather than to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I wish that what the dream and its interpretation predict would happen to those who hate you, your enemies, rather than to you]

Belteshazzar is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [My lord, may the dream be for the ones hating you and may its interpretation be for your enemies]

22.note: Here Daniel is speaking as if the king were the tree that Nebuchadnezzar saw in his dream. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that tree is a symbol of you, O king]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **greatness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And how great you are has increased]

Daniel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and your dominion has reached to the end of the earth]

25.q: וְ⁠לָ֣⁠ךְ טָֽרְדִ֣ין מִן־אֲנָשָׁ֡⁠א & וְ⁠עִשְׂבָּ֥⁠א כְ⁠תוֹרִ֣ין ׀ לָ֣⁠ךְ יְטַֽעֲמ֗וּן וּ⁠מִ⁠טַּ֤ל שְׁמַיָּ⁠א֙ לָ֣⁠ךְ מְצַבְּעִ֔ין
25.note: In each of these instances, the pronoun **they** does not refer to specific people. Daniel is using it to describe what will happen to the king. In some languages, it may be natural to use passive verbal forms to express this meaning. Alternate translation: [you will be driven from men … And you will be fed grass like oxen, and you will be wetted with the dew of the heavens]

The point of this comparison is that just as **oxen** eat **grass**, so the king will be made to eat grass. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And they will make you eat grass, just as oxen eat grass]

Daniel is using **And seven times will pass over you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “seven years will pass for you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Seven years will go by for you] or [This will continue for seven years]

26.q: וְ⁠דִ֣י אֲמַ֗רוּ לְ⁠מִשְׁבַּ֞ק עִקַּ֤ר שָׁרְשׁ֨וֹ⁠הִי֙ דִּ֣י אִֽילָנָ֔⁠א מַלְכוּתָ֖⁠ךְ לָ֣⁠ךְ קַיָּמָ֑ה
26.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the king’s kingdom enduring before the information about leaving the stump of the roots of the tree. Alternate translation: [And your kingdom will be an enduring kingdom for you; that is what they meant when they said to leave the stump of the roots of the tree]
Here, **the heavens** represents “God.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [God is ruler]

27.note: Here Daniel is speaking as if the king could **break off** his sin the way a person breaks off a branch from a tree. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and may you cease from your sin by doing what is right and from your iniquities]

Here, the term **if** marks a prolonging of your prosperity as the possible result of Nebuchadnezzar breaking off his sin to practice righteousness and his iniquity by showing mercy to the poor. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that Daniel is suggesting that this could be a result. Alternate translation: [so that]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by doing what is right]

Daniel is using the adjective **the poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are poor]

28.note: Nebuchadnezzar is the one telling this account, but he speaks of himself in the third person as **King Nebuchadnezzar**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [Everything from the dream came upon me, King Nebuchadnezzar]

29.note: Nebuchadnezzar is using the phrase translated as **At the end of 12 months** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

30.q: הֲ⁠לָ֥א דָא־הִ֖יא בָּבֶ֣ל רַבְּתָ֑⁠א דִּֽי־אֲנָ֤ה בֱנַיְתַ⁠הּ֙ לְ⁠בֵ֣ית מַלְכ֔וּ בִּ⁠תְקַ֥ף חִסְנִ֖⁠י וְ⁠לִ⁠יקָ֥ר הַדְרִֽ⁠י
30.note: Nebuchadnezzar is using the question form to boast about what he has accomplished. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This is indeed the great Babylon, which I myself have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty!]

It might seem that the expression **which I, I have built it** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [which I have built]

Nebuchadnezzar is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **have built** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one who built this great city, showing his pride in his own achievement. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [which I myself have built it]

31.note: Nebuchadnezzar is using the expression **still in the mouth of the king** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the king was still speaking.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The king was still speaking these words]

33.q: וּ⁠מִן־אֲנָשָׁ֣⁠א טְרִ֔יד וְ⁠עִשְׂבָּ֤⁠א כְ⁠תוֹרִין֙ יֵאכֻ֔ל וּ⁠מִ⁠טַּ֥ל שְׁמַיָּ֖⁠א גִּשְׁמֵ֣⁠הּ יִצְטַבַּ֑ע
33.note: The expressions **was driven** and **was wet** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And people drove him away from man, and he ate grass like oxen, and the dew of the heavens made his body wet]

The point of this comparison is that just as **eagles** have long feathers and **birds** have long claws, so the king’s hair and nails grew very long. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [his hair had grown very long, as long as the feathers of eagles, and his nails had grown very long, as long as the claws of birds]

35.note: The expression **are being regarded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And God regards all of the dwellers of the earth as nothing]

Here Nebuchadnezzar is speaking as if the beings in the heavens were an **army**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among the beings who live in the heavens]

Nebuchadnezzar is using the expression **strikes his hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean “restrains him or stops him from acting.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And there is none who holds him back]

Anyone who would say this to God would be using the question form to challenge or rebuke him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have no right to do this!]

36.q: וְ⁠עַל־מַלְכוּתִ֣⁠י הָתְקְנַ֔ת וּ⁠רְב֥וּ יַתִּירָ֖ה ה֥וּסְפַת לִֽ⁠י
36.note: The expressions **was established** and **was added** are passive verbal forms. If it would be unnatural to use those forms, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God established my kingdom for me and gave exceeding greatness to me]

37.note: The terms **praising** and **exalting** and **glorifying** mean similar things. Nebuchadnezzar is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [am greatly praising the King of the heavens]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [all of his deeds are true]

Here Nebuchadnezzar is speaking as if the way God acts were the **ways** or paths on which God travels. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and everything he does is just]

Here Nebuchadnezzar is speaking as if the ways people behave were **walking about**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and those who conduct themselves with pride]
